Study sections in order of priority: VERY HIGH and HIGH first, then MEDIUM, then LOW.
For every section: read 'must_know', memorise the 'key_provisions' table, then revise 'landmark_cases' (case name + one-line ratio).
AIBE is an open-book exam: knowing WHERE an Article sits in the Bare Act is as valuable as memorising it. Tab your Constitution by Part.
Finish with 'latest_developments', 'rapid_revision' and the 'mcq_bank'. Re-attempt the MCQs after 7 days.

exam_intelligence.distribution_note: This distribution is an indicative estimate built from the pattern of past AIBE papers and syllabus weight; BCI does not publish a topic-wise split.
question_patterns: Direct recall: 'Which Article deals with ...?' / 'Which Amendment inserted ...?'
Case-to-principle matching: 'Doctrine of basic structure was propounded in ...'
Statement-based: 'Which of the following statements is/are correct?' (1, 2, 3 combinations)
Negative framing: 'Which of the following is NOT a fundamental right?'

Current-affairs tie-in: recent Constitution Bench ruling or recent amendment bill
Short fact-based scenarios (Governor/Speaker/President action - is it valid?)

Art 14 reasonable classification and arbitrariness test

time_strategy: Target about 90 seconds per Constitutional Law question; these are mostly recall questions, so bank time here for the lengthy CPC/CrPC/Evidence problems.
Because AIBE is open-book, mark the Constitution Bare Act with Part-wise flags and keep a one-page index of case names with years.
Do not spend time reading long Article text for a question you can answer from memory; use the book only to confirm numbers, periods and clauses.
common_traps: Art 21A (education 6-14) vs Art 45 (early childhood care under 6) vs Art 51A(k) (parent's duty).
Right to property is NOT a fundamental right since the 44th Amendment (Art 300A is a constitutional right).
Right to vote and right to contest are statutory/constitutional rights, not fundamental rights.
Right to strike, right to bandh, right to be heard in every case are not fundamental rights.
Art 19 is available only to citizens; Art 14, 20, 21, 22 (partly), 25 are available to non-citizens too.
Art 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during Emergency (44th Amendment); Art 19 is suspended only under war/external aggression emergency (Art 358).
The Preamble was amended only once (42nd Amendment, 1976).
Berubari (1960) said Preamble is not part of the Constitution; Kesavananda (1973) said it is part.
Governor cannot pardon a death sentence, but can suspend, remit or commute it (Art 161).
Money Bill cannot be introduced in Rajya Sabha; joint sitting under Art 108 does not apply to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills.

sections.title: Making of the Constitution, Salient Features and the Preamble
sections.overview: Foundation topic. Questions are factual: dates, persons, sources of borrowed features, Preamble keywords and the Preamble cases.
must_know: Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946). First meeting: 9 December 1946. Dr Sachchidananda Sinha was provisional president; Dr Rajendra Prasad became permanent president (11 Dec 1946).
Objectives (Objective) Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946; adopted 22 January 1947.
Drafting Committee set up 29 August 1947 under Dr B.R. Ambedkar (7 members). B.N. Rau was Constitutional Adviser.

Constitution adopted 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day / Samvidhan Divas); fully in force 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). Certain provisions (citizenship, elections, interim Parliament, etc.: Arts 5-9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393) came into force on 26 Nov 1949.
Original Constitution: 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules. Present count: about 448 Articles, 25 Parts, 12 Schedules.

Preamble: 'We, the people of India' - Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; secures Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status, opportunity), Fraternity (dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation).
'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). This is the only amendment to the Preamble.
Preamble is neither a source of power nor a limitation on power, and is non-justiciable, but it is an aid to interpretation.

Nature of polity: Union of States; federal in form with a strong unitary bias (quasi-federal); parliamentary government; independent integrated judiciary; single citizenship; universal adult suffrage (age 18 after the 61st Amendment, 1988).

key_provisions.content: Key words: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic. Date of adoption mentioned: 26 November 1949.

UK: parliamentary system, rule of law, single citizenship, cabinet system, writs, bicameralism, Speaker. USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, impeachment, Vice-President, Preamble. Ireland: DPSP, nomination to Rajya Sabha, method of Presidential election. Canada: federation with strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction. Australia: Concurrent List, freedom of trade (Part XIII), joint sitting. Germany (Weimar): suspension of FR during Emergency. USSR: Fundamental Duties. France: Republic; ideals of Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. South Africa: procedure for amendment, election of Rajya Sabha members. Japan: procedure established by law. Government of India Act 1935: federal scheme, Governor's office, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions, administrative details.

landmark_cases.case: In re Berubari Union (Reference under Art 143)
landmark_cases.held: Preamble is not a part of the Constitution; it is a key to the minds of the framers. Cession of Indian territory requires a Constitution amendment under Art 368.

landmark_cases.case: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
landmark_cases.held: Preamble IS a part of the Constitution and can be amended, subject to the basic structure.

landmark_cases.case: LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre
landmark_cases.held: Reaffirmed that Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.

landmark_cases.case: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution; State must maintain equal distance from all religions.

landmark_cases.case: Kesavananda Bharati (supremacy principle)
landmark_cases.held: Sovereignty vests in the people; the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme.

mnemonics: Preamble keywords: 'S-S-S-D-R' = Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
Justice-Liberty-Equality-Fraternity: 'JLEF'.
exam_traps: India is described as 'Union of States' (Art 1) - not a 'federation'; the word 'federal' is not used in the Constitution.
Date the Constitution was adopted (26 Nov 1949) differs from the date it commenced (26 Jan 1950).
probable_questions: Which Amendment added the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble?
In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is part of the Constitution?
Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee?

sections.title: Union and its Territory; Citizenship (Arts 1-11)
sections.overview: Short but factual. Art 3 mechanics, Art 2 vs Art 3, Citizenship Act 1955 modes and the CAA/Section 6A developments are the usual testing points.
must_know: Art 1: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'. Territory = States, Union Territories, and territories that may be acquired.
Art 2: Parliament may admit into the Union or establish NEW States (not part of India) - e.g., Sikkim (1975, 35th and 36th Amendments).

Art 3: Parliament may by law form new States, alter areas, boundaries or names of existing States. Procedure: Bill only on President's recommendation; President refers it to the State Legislature concerned for its views (not binding - Babulal Parante, 1960); simple majority; not an Art 368 amendment (Art 4).
Art 4: laws under Arts 2 and 3 are not constitutional amendments under Art 368.
Present position: 28 States and 8 Union Territories (J&K reorganised as UT in 2019; Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu merged in 2020). Telangana (2014) is the youngest State.

Citizenship in Constitution: Art 5 (domicile at commencement), Art 6 (migrants from Pakistan), Art 7 (migrants to Pakistan who returned), Art 8 (persons of Indian origin abroad), Art 9 (voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship = loss), Art 10 (continuance), Art 11 (Parliament's power to regulate citizenship by law).

Citizenship Act 1955: acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory. Loss: renunciation, termination (voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship), deprivation.

Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019: gives fast-track path (residence 5 years) to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014. Rules notified in March 2024.
Section 6A (Assam Accord migrants who entered between 1 Jan 1966 and 25 Mar 1971) was upheld by a Constitution Bench in Oct 2024 (4:1).

key_provisions.content: Bill needs President's recommendation + reference to State Legislature (for effect on a State's area/boundaries/name).
Parliament has plenary power to make law on acquisition and termination of citizenship.

landmark_cases.case: Berubari Union (1960)
landmark_cases.held: Art 3 does not cover cession of territory to a foreign State; Art 368 amendment required.

landmark_cases.case: Babulal Parante v. State of Bombay
landmark_cases.held: State Legislature's views under Art 3 are not binding on Parliament; fresh reference not needed after amendments to the Bill.

landmark_cases.case: State of Arunachal Pradesh v. Khudiram Chakma
landmark_cases.held: Chakma refugees are entitled to life and personal liberty; State must protect them.

landmark_cases.case: Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: IMDT Act struck down; Assam faced 'external aggression' through illegal migration.

landmark_cases.case: In re Section 6A, Citizenship Act
landmark_cases.held: Constitution Bench (4:1) upheld Section 6A as a valid legislative solution for Assam.

exam_traps: Art 3 changes do not need a special majority or State ratification.
Citizenship under Part II is a Union subject (List I, Entry 17); States have no say.
probable_questions: Parliament's power to form a new State derives from which Article?
Which Article provides that law made under Art 3 is not an amendment under Art 368?
Consequences of voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship?

sections.title: Amendment of the Constitution (Art 368) and the Basic Structure Doctrine
sections.overview: A perennial AIBE favourite. Know: the three methods of amendment, the evolution Shankari Prasad -> Golak Nath -> Kesavananda -> Minerva Mills -> Waman Rao -> I.R. Coelho, and what counts as basic structure. Also know the important Amendment Acts and their numbers.
must_know: Art 368 (as amended by the 24th Amendment, 1971): Parliament's constituent power; amendment by introducing a Bill in either House; no prior sanction; President MUST give assent (24th Amendment); no joint sitting for deadlock.

Method 1 - SIMPLE MAJORITY (outside Art 368): admission/establishment of new States (Arts 2-4), Legislative Councils (Art 169), citizenship, Fifth and Sixth Schedules, Art 239A/240, languages, quorum, salaries of MPs, etc.

Method 2 - SPECIAL MAJORITY: majority of total membership of each House + two-thirds of members present and voting. Applies to all fundamental rights, DPSPs and all provisions not under Methods 1 and 3.

Method 3 - SPECIAL MAJORITY + RATIFICATION BY AT LEAST HALF OF THE STATE LEGISLATURES: election of President (Arts 54, 55), extent of executive power of Union/States (Arts 73, 162), Supreme Court and High Courts (Chapters IV of Part V and V of Part VI), Union Territories' High Courts (Art 241), legislative relations (Ch I Part XI), Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, Art 368 itself, GST Council (Art 279A) provisions of the 101st Amendment.
Basic structure doctrine: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot destroy or alter its basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, 13 judges, 7:6).

Features recognised as basic: supremacy of the Constitution; rule of law; separation of powers; judicial review (Arts 32, 226, 227); independence of judiciary; federalism; secularism; sovereign democratic republic; parliamentary democracy; free and fair elections; unity and integrity of the nation; equality (Art 14 core); harmony and balance between FR and DPSP; limited amending power of Parliament; Art 32 access to Supreme Court; welfare state; essence of FR.

Not held to be basic structure (illustrative): right to property; Art 356 power is subject to review, not itself 'basic'; ordinary legislation cannot be struck merely for violating basic structure (Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975; State of Karnataka v. Union of India, 1977 - basic structure tests constitutional amendments, not ordinary laws).

Ninth Schedule (inserted by the 1st Amendment, 1951 via Art 31B): laws placed here were immune from judicial review. After I.R. Coelho (2007), laws placed after 24 April 1973 are open to review on the touchstone of basic structure and Part III.

Art 31C (25th Amendment, 1971): laws giving effect to Art 39(b)/(c) immune from challenge under Arts 14, 19, 31. Kesavananda upheld the first part and struck the 'declaration is final' clause. 42nd Amendment extended it to ALL DPSPs - struck down in Minerva Mills (1980). Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (Nov 2024, 9 judges) confirmed that Art 31C as upheld in Kesavananda survives.

key_provisions.content: Constituent power of Parliament to amend by way of addition, variation or repeal (inserted by 24th Amendment).
Special majority + ratification where required; President shall give assent.
Nothing in Art 13 shall apply to any amendment under this Article (24th Amendment).
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment (no amendment can be questioned in court; unlimited amending power); struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).
13(2): no law shall take away or abridge FR; 13(4) added by the 24th Amendment: Art 13 does not apply to Art 368 amendments.

1st (1951) Ninth Schedule, Art 15(4), 19(2) additions; 7th (1956) reorganisation of States; 24th (1971) amending power; 25th (1971) Art 31C; 42nd (1976) 'mini-Constitution': Preamble, FDs (Art 51A), DPSP changes, Art 368(4)-(5); 44th (1978) property removed from Part III, Art 300A, Emergency safeguards; 52nd (1985) Tenth Schedule; 61st (1988) voting age 18; 69th (1991) Delhi NCT; 73rd and 74th (1992) local governments; 86th (2002) Art 21A; 91st (2003) 15% ministers cap, anti-defection tightening; 97th (2011) cooperatives; 99th (2014) NJAC (struck down 2015); 101st (2016) GST; 102nd (2018) NCBC constitutional status; 103rd (2019) EWS reservation; 104th (2020) SC/ST reservation in legislatures extended, Anglo-Indian seats ended; 105th (2021) States' power to identify SEBCs restored; 106th (2023) women's reservation (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam).

landmark_cases.case: Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights; 'law' in Art 13 does not include constitutional amendments.

landmark_cases.case: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan
landmark_cases.held: Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad (3:2); Hidayatullah and Mudholkar JJ. doubted if basic features could be amended.

landmark_cases.case: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
landmark_cases.held: 11 judges, 6:5. Parliament cannot amend Part III; constitutional amendment is 'law' under Art 13(2). Applied prospective overruling.

landmark_cases.case: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
landmark_cases.held: 13 judges, 7:6. Overruled Golak Nath. Parliament can amend any provision but not the 'basic structure'. Longest hearing (68 days).

landmark_cases.case: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
landmark_cases.held: Art 329A(4) (inserted by the 39th Amendment) struck down - free and fair elections, rule of law and judicial review are basic features.

landmark_cases.case: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Struck down Sec 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment (Art 31C extension and Art 368(4)-(5)). Harmony between FR and DPSP is basic structure; 'limited amending power is itself a basic feature'.

landmark_cases.case: Waman Rao v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Cut-off 24 April 1973: amendments to Ninth Schedule before that date are valid; after that open to review.

landmark_cases.case: S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Tribunal as substitute for HC upheld (later modified by L. Chandra Kumar).

landmark_cases.case: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Power of judicial review of HC and SC (Arts 226/227/32) is basic structure; tribunals' decisions subject to HC scrutiny.

landmark_cases.case: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
landmark_cases.held: 9 judges. Ninth Schedule laws are not beyond judicial review if they damage basic structure or Arts 14, 19, 21 core.

landmark_cases.case: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Fourth Judges case)
landmark_cases.held: 99th Amendment and NJAC Act struck down (4:1); collegium system restored; independence of judiciary is basic structure.

landmark_cases.case: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: 103rd Amendment (10% EWS reservation, Arts 15(6), 16(6)) upheld 3:2. Economic criterion alone can be a ground; 50% ceiling applies to existing reservations only.

landmark_cases.case: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra
landmark_cases.held: 9 judges: 'material resources of the community' in Art 39(b) does not automatically include all privately owned resources; Art 31C as upheld in Kesavananda remains good law.

mnemonics: Chronology: 'S-S-G-K-M' = Shankari (1951), Sajjan (1965), Golak Nath (1967), Kesavananda (1973), Minerva (1980).
Special majority = 'Majority of the total + 2/3 of present and voting'. Remember the word TOTAL.
exam_traps: Number of judges in Kesavananda = 13; majority 7:6 (a razor-thin margin).
Golak Nath = 11 judges (6:5).
Basic structure is not found in the text - judge-made. Art 368 has no express mention.
The Preamble can be amended (done once, by the 42nd Amendment) but not so as to alter the basic structure.
probable_questions: In which case did the Supreme Court first lay down the doctrine of basic structure?
Which amendment inserted Art 368(4) and (5), and what happened to it in Minerva Mills?
Ninth Schedule laws placed after which date are open to judicial review?
Which of the following requires ratification by half of the States?

sections.title: Fundamental Rights: Arts 12 and 13 (State, Law, Doctrines)
sections.overview: Gateway to Part III. 'State' under Art 12 and doctrines of eclipse, severability, waiver and pre/post-constitutional laws are frequent MCQ material.
must_know: Art 12: 'State' includes Government and Parliament of India, Government and Legislature of each State, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

'Other authorities' (Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal, 1967): authorities exercising governmental or sovereign functions/with statutory power to make rules. Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram (1975): statutory corporations (LIC, ONGC) are State. Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981): functional-institutional tests - deep and pervasive State control, financial aid, monopoly status, governmental functions. Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (2002): 'dominant control' test.

Judiciary: courts acting in judicial capacity are not 'State' for Art 12 for writ of certiorari against judicial orders (Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002; Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar, 1966) - but administrative functions of courts are covered.

BCCI is not 'State' (Zee Telefilms v. Union of India, 2005) but its public functions can be reviewed under Art 226. Private banks are not 'State' (Federal Bank v. Sagar Thomas, 2003) though writ may lie for public duty.

Art 13(1): pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with FR are void to the extent of inconsistency (doctrine of eclipse: they become dormant, not dead - Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P., 1955). Art 13(2): State cannot make law violating FR; such a law is void to the extent (ab initio - Deep Chand v. State of U.P., 1959). Post-Constitution law violating FR guaranteed only to citizens is void only vis-a-vis citizens and operative for non-citizens (State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills, 1974).

Art 13(3): 'law' includes ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having force of law. Art 13(4): constitutional amendments under Art 368 are not 'law' (24th Amendment).
Doctrine of severability: only the unconstitutional part is struck if it is severable (A.K. Gopalan, 1950; R.M.D.C. v. Union of India, 1957).
Doctrine of waiver: Fundamental rights cannot be waived (Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v. State of Bombay, 1955; Basheshar Nath v. CIT, 1959; Olga Tellis, 1985).
Rights available only to citizens: Art 15, 16, 19, 29, 30. Available to all persons: Art 14, 20, 21, 21A (children), 22, 23, 24, 25-28 (religion), 32.

Rights enforceable against private persons: Art 15(2), 17, 23, 24 (horizontal effect). Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023): FRs under Arts 19 and 21 can also be enforced against non-State actors in appropriate cases.

key_provisions.content: Definition of 'State' for Part III.
Pre-constitutional laws, to the extent of inconsistency, are void.
Post-constitutional laws, to the extent of contravention, are void.
'Law' defined; 'laws in force' defined.
Amendment under Art 368 is not 'law' under Art 13.

landmark_cases.case: Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal
landmark_cases.held: Wide interpretation of 'other authorities'.

landmark_cases.case: Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagat Ram
landmark_cases.held: Statutory corporations are 'State'.

landmark_cases.case: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi
landmark_cases.held: Five-factor test for 'instrumentality or agency of State'.

landmark_cases.case: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. IICB
landmark_cases.held: Overruled the narrow Sabhajit Tewary; 'dominant control' test.

landmark_cases.case: Zee Telefilms v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: BCCI not 'State', but writ may lie for public duties.

landmark_cases.case: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P.
landmark_cases.held: Doctrine of eclipse - pre-constitution law not dead but dormant.

landmark_cases.case: Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v. State of Bombay
landmark_cases.held: No waiver of FR.

landmark_cases.case: Deep Chand v. State of U.P.
landmark_cases.held: Post-constitution law violating Art 13(2) is stillborn/void ab initio.

landmark_cases.case: Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P.
landmark_cases.held: FR under Arts 19/21 are enforceable against private persons; no additional restrictions on Art 19(1)(a) beyond Art 19(2).

exam_traps: Eclipse vs severability: eclipse deals with timing (revival when obstruction removed); severability deals with extent (part void).
Doctrine of eclipse for post-constitution laws applies only in respect of non-citizens.
probable_questions: Which test is used to decide whether a body is 'State' under Art 12?
Doctrine of eclipse was propounded in which case?
Which Fundamental Rights are available against private individuals?

sections.title: Right to Equality (Arts 14-18) and Reservation Jurisprudence
sections.overview: Art 14 tests (classification and arbitrariness), Art 15/16 clauses with the amendments that added them, Indra Sawhney (and its progeny) and Art 17/18 basics.
must_know: Art 14: 'equality before law' (British/Dicey - negative, no special privilege) + 'equal protection of laws' (American - positive, equals treated alike). Available to all persons including corporations.

Reasonable classification test (State of W.B. v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952; Ram Krishna Dalmia, 1958): (i) intelligible differentia; (ii) rational nexus with the object. Presumption of constitutionality lies on the law.
New concept of equality - arbitrariness is antithesis of equality (E.P. Royappa v. State of T.N., 1974; Maneka Gandhi, 1978). Ajay Hasia (1981) extended to administrative action.

Manifest arbitrariness as ground to strike down legislation: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) (instant triple talaq void); Navtej Singh Johar (2018); Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) (adultery, s.497 IPC, struck down).
Exceptions to Art 14: President and Governors (Art 361); privileges of legislators (Arts 105, 194); foreign sovereigns and diplomats; Art 31C.
Equal pay for equal work: Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982) (derived from Arts 14, 16, 39(d)).

Art 15(1): State shall not discriminate on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. Art 15(2): access to shops, public restaurants, wells, tanks, roads - binds even private persons. Art 15(3): special provisions for women and children. Art 15(4): SEBC/SC/ST (1st Amendment, 1951 after State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan). Art 15(5): admissions to educational institutions including private unaided (93rd Amendment, 2005) - except minority institutions (Pramati Educational Trust, 2014). Art 15(6): EWS (103rd Amendment, 2019).

Art 16(1): equality of opportunity in public employment; 16(2): no discrimination only on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence; 16(3): Parliament may prescribe residence requirement (only Parliament, not State); 16(4): reservation for backward classes not adequately represented; 16(4A): promotions for SC/ST (77th Amendment, 1995); 16(4B): carry-forward of unfilled vacancies (81st Amendment, 2000); 16(5): office-bearers of religious institutions; 16(6): EWS (103rd Amendment).

Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), 9 judges, 6:3: upheld 27% OBC reservation (Mandal); excluded 'creamy layer'; 50% ceiling on total reservations (barring extraordinary situations); no reservation in promotions (prospectively, 5 years - later overridden by 77th Amendment for SC/ST); Art 16(4) is not an exception to 16(1); economic criterion alone cannot define backwardness (EWS later enabled through 103rd Amendment).

M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006): upheld 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments subject to conditions (quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequacy of representation, efficiency). Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018): no need for quantifiable data of backwardness for SC/ST; need for inadequacy data remains.

State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (1 Aug 2024), 7 judges, 6:1: sub-classification of Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes for granting preferential reservation is permissible; overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004); some judges opined that creamy layer should apply to SC/ST.

Dr Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister (2021): Maratha reservation struck down; 50% ceiling reaffirmed; 102nd Amendment (Art 342A) removed States' power to identify SEBCs - later restored by 105th Amendment (2021).

Art 17: abolition of untouchability; Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 (earlier Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955), plus SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989. Art 17 is enforceable against private persons.

Art 18: abolishes titles; no citizen can accept title from foreign State; exception: military and academic distinctions. Bharat Ratna/Padma awards are not titles (Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India, 1996).

key_provisions.content: State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
EWS reservation up to 10% in addition to existing reservations; not available to SEBC/SC/ST already covered.
Reservation in matters of promotion with consequential seniority for SC/ST.
Claims of SC/ST to services to be considered consistent with maintenance of efficiency of administration.
National Commission for SC / ST / Backward Classes (102nd Amendment gave NCBC constitutional status).
340: Commission to investigate conditions of backward classes; 341: SC list by President; 342: ST list; 342A: SEBC list by President (102nd), State power restored by 105th Amendment.

landmark_cases.case: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
landmark_cases.held: Special courts act struck for unguided classification.

landmark_cases.case: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
landmark_cases.held: Communal G.O. struck down; led to 1st Amendment (Art 15(4)).

landmark_cases.case: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu

sections.title: Right to Freedom: Art 19 (Six Freedoms) and Reasonable Restrictions
sections.overview: Know each freedom, the corresponding restriction clause and the grounds. Free speech cases (Romesh Thappar, Shreya Singhal, Anuradha Bhasin, Kaushal Kishor, Electoral Bonds) are hot.
must_know: Art 19(1) (citizens only): (a) speech and expression; (b) assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) form associations or unions or co-operative societies (97th Amendment); (d) move freely throughout India; (e) reside and settle anywhere; (g) practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business. (f) (property) was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978).

Art 19(2) grounds for 19(1)(a): sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence. ('Public order' added by 1st Amendment 1951; 'sovereignty and integrity' by 16th Amendment 1963.)

Art 19(3): restrictions on 19(1)(b) - sovereignty, integrity and public order. Art 19(4): on 19(1)(c) - same grounds + morality. Art 19(5): on 19(1)(d),(e) - general public interest + protection of Scheduled Tribes. Art 19(6): on 19(1)(g) - public interest; professional or technical qualifications; State monopolies.

Restrictions must be 'reasonable' - both substantive and procedural reasonableness (State of Madras v. V.G. Row, 1952). Test of proportionality applied (Modern Dental College, 2016; Puttaswamy, 2017; Anuradha Bhasin, 2020).

Freedom of speech includes: freedom of press (Romesh Thappar, 1950; Sakal Papers, 1962); right to circulate (Bennett Coleman, 1973); right to know / information (Raj Narain, 1975; S.P. Gupta, 1981); right to know candidates' antecedents (ADR, 2002; PUCL, 2003); right to broadcast (Cricket Association of Bengal, 1995); freedom of silence (Bijoe Emmanuel, 1986); right to fly the national flag (Naveen Jindal, 2004); commercial speech (Tata Press, 1995); internet access in a restricted manner (Anuradha Bhasin, 2020); right to criticise.

No fundamental right to strike (T.K. Rangarajan v. Govt of T.N., 2003), no right to bandh (Communist Party of India (M) v. Bharat Kumar, 1998). No right to hold demonstrations on public roads indefinitely (Amit Sahni, 2020).
Obscenity: Ranjit Udeshi (1965) Hicklin test; Aveek Sarkar v. State of W.B. (2014) shifted to 'community standards' test.

Hate speech / sedition: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962) upheld sedition (s.124A IPC) with incitement to violence requirement; Supreme Court kept s.124A in abeyance in S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (May 2022). BNS 2023 does not contain sedition but s.152 punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
Defamation: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) upheld criminal defamation (ss.499/500 IPC).
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015): s.66A IT Act struck down as vague and overbroad; s.69A upheld; s.79 read down; distinction between discussion, advocacy and incitement.

Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020): freedom of speech on internet and the right to carry on trade via internet enjoy Art 19 protection; indefinite internet shutdown impermissible; orders must be published and be proportionate.

Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023): grounds in Art 19(2) are exhaustive - no additional restrictions on free speech can be imposed (e.g., by invoking Art 21); Art 19/21 rights can have horizontal effect.
Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (15 Feb 2024): Electoral Bond Scheme struck down as violating voters' right to information under Art 19(1)(a).

Right to practise profession includes the right not to practise (Art 19(1)(g)); no right to carry on trade in 'res extra commercium' like liquor (State of Punjab v. Devans Modern Breweries, 2003); State monopolies protected under Art 19(6)(ii).
Right to move and reside: right to travel abroad is not in Art 19 - it is part of personal liberty under Art 21 (Satwant Singh Sawhney, 1967; Maneka Gandhi, 1978).

key_provisions.content: Freedom of speech and expression (includes press, information, silence).
Eight grounds of restriction - memorise: sovereignty & integrity, security of State, friendly relations, public order, decency/morality, contempt, defamation, incitement.
State can impose restrictions, set professional qualifications, and carry on trade itself/exclude citizens (monopoly).

sections.title: Protection in Criminal Proceedings, Right to Life and Personal Liberty, Arrest and Detention (Arts 20, 21, 21A, 22)
sections.overview: The single most important cluster. Art 21's expansion through Maneka Gandhi, Puttaswamy and several 'rights included' cases is repeatedly asked. Art 22's numbers (24 hours, 3 months) are classic. Cross-refer CrPC/BNSS (Part 2).
must_know: Art 20(1) - no ex post facto criminal law (conviction or greater penalty than law at the time); applies only to criminal laws (Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab, 1964); does not bar retrospective procedural/ civil laws. Art 20(2) - no double jeopardy (prosecution and punishment for same offence only once) - applies only to judicial proceedings (Maqbool Hussain, 1953) - departmental inquiry then trial is no bar. Art 20(3) - no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be witness against himself.

Art 20(3) requirements: accused person; compulsion; testimonial evidence. Samples like fingerprints, handwriting, thumb impression are not testimonial (State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad, 1961, 11 judges). Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978): right to silence extends to police interrogation. Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010): narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping without consent violate Arts 20(3) and 21. Ritesh Sinha v. State of U.P. (2019): magistrate may order voice samples.

Art 21: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' A.K. Gopalan (1950) - narrow, procedure merely 'enacted by legislature'. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) - procedure must be just, fair and reasonable; Arts 14, 19, 21 form a 'golden triangle'; right to travel abroad is part of Art 21.

Art 21 includes (illustrative): right to live with human dignity (Francis Coralie Mullin, 1981); livelihood (Olga Tellis, 1985); speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979); free legal aid (M.H. Hoskot, 1978; Hussainara); against solitary confinement and bar fetters (Sunil Batra, 1978; Prem Shankar Shukla, 1980); privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017); health and emergency medical aid (Parmanand Katara, 1989; Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity, 1996); clean environment (Subhash Kumar, 1991; M.C. Mehta); shelter; education (Unni Krishnan, 1993); freedom from sexual harassment at work (Vishaka, 1997); reputation (Kiran Bedi); marriage of choice (Shafin Jahan, 2018; Shakti Vahini, 2018); passive euthanasia and living will (Common Cause, 2018; Aruna Shanbaug, 2011); against custodial violence and arrest guidelines (D.K. Basu, 1997); against delay in executing death sentence (Shatrughan Chauhan, 2014); right to be forgotten; right against climate change harms (M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024); right to digital access for persons with disabilities and acid-attack survivors (Amar Jain v. Union of India, 2025); reproductive autonomy incl. for unmarried women (X v. Principal Secretary, Health, 2022); menstrual health reported recognised as part of Art 21 (Jan 2026) [VERIFY case title].

Right to die: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996) - right to life does not include right to die; euthanasia (passive) permitted under strict guidelines (Common Cause). BNS 2023 has no counterpart of s.309 IPC (attempted suicide); Mental Healthcare Act 2017, s.115, presumes severe stress.

Death penalty: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) upheld constitutionality, 'rarest of rare' doctrine; Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) struck down mandatory death penalty (s.303 IPC); Machhi Singh (1983) categories; Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) - inordinate delay can commute.

Right to privacy: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (24 Aug 2017), 9 judges, unanimous: privacy is a fundamental right under Art 21 (and Part III as a whole); overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) in part; ADM Jabalpur (1976) declared wrongly decided. Puttaswamy-II (2018): Aadhaar Act upheld (4:1) with s.57 struck and limits.

Art 21A (86th Amendment 2002; RTE Act 2009 in force 1 April 2010): free and compulsory education for children 6-14 years; RTE Act s.12(1)(c) 25% quota in private unaided schools upheld in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan (2012); Pramati (2014): RTE Act not applicable to minority schools.

Art 22(1)-(2) (arrest): right to be informed of grounds; consult and be defended by legal practitioner of choice; production before nearest Magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time. Not available to enemy aliens and persons detained under preventive detention laws.

Art 22(3)-(7) (preventive detention): no detention beyond 3 months unless Advisory Board (judges or persons qualified as HC judges) reports sufficient cause; grounds to be communicated; earliest opportunity of representation; Parliament may prescribe maximum period (e.g., 12 months in National Security Act 1980). 44th Amendment proposed 2 months and Advisory Board chaired by HC judge but is not yet brought into force. A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982): NSA valid; no right to counsel before Advisory Board. Preventive detention is a concurrent subject (Entry 9 List I - defence/foreign; Entry 3 List III - others).

Arrest law linkages: Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994), D.K. Basu v. State of W.B. (1997), Arnesh Kumar (2014), Hussainara; Court on handcuffing (Prem Shankar Shukla); bail under Art 21 (Satender Kumar Antil, 2022; Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb, 2021 - prolonged incarceration violates Art 21 even under UAPA).

key_provisions.content: No conviction except for violation of law in force at the time; no penalty greater than that prescribed at the time.
No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.
No accused shall be compelled to be witness against himself.
Protection of life and personal liberty.
Right to education (6-14).
Production before Magistrate within 24 hours.
Preventive detention beyond three months only with Advisory Board report.
Presidential order can suspend enforcement of FR during Emergency except Arts 20 and 21 (44th Amendment).

sections.title: Rights against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights (Arts 23-30)
sections.overview: Art 25-26 is currently a hot area due to the nine-judge Sabarimala reference. Art 30 minority educational institutions (TMA Pai, AMU) is a regular question.
must_know: Art 23: prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forced labour; operates against private persons also; State may impose compulsory service for public purposes (without discrimination). PUDR v. Union of India (1982, Asiad workers): non-payment of minimum wages = forced labour. Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984).

Art 24: no child below 14 to be employed in factory, mine or hazardous employment. Cross-refer: Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, as amended in 2016 (prohibits employment of children below 14 in all occupations; adolescents (14-18) in hazardous work).

Art 25(1): freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion - subject to public order, morality, health and other FR; Art 25(2)(a) State can regulate economic, financial, political or secular activity associated with religion; 25(2)(b) social welfare and reform and throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus. Explanation: Sikhs' kirpan; Hindu includes Sikh, Jain, Buddhist.

'Propagate' does not include right to convert (Rev. Stanislaus v. State of M.P., 1977) - anti-conversion laws upheld; 'essential religious practices' test: Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar (Shirur Mutt), 1954; Durgah Committee, Ajmer v. Syed Hussain Ali (1961) - protection only to practices essential and integral; Ismail Faruqui v. Union of India (1994): mosque not essential to Islam; Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala, 2018): 4:1, exclusion of women aged 10-50 from Sabarimala temple unconstitutional (Indu Malhotra J. dissented); review in Kantaru Rajeevaru (2019) referred broad questions to a larger bench; nine-judge bench heard the reference (Apr-May 2026) and judgment is reserved [VERIFY if pronounced].

Art 26: freedom to manage religious affairs for every religious denomination - (a) establish and maintain institutions for religious/charitable purposes; (b) manage its own affairs in matters of religion; (c) own and acquire property; (d) administer property per law. Denomination = a religious sect with distinct organisation, name and common faith (Shirur Mutt). Art 26 is subject to public order, morality and health only (not to other FR, per some decisions - being reconsidered in Sabarimala reference).

Art 27: no person compelled to pay taxes for promotion/maintenance of any particular religion. Art 28: no religious instruction in State-funded institutions (28(1)); permitted in institutions administered by the State under endowment/trust requiring it (28(2)); attendance voluntary in recognised/aided institutions (28(3)). Aruna Roy v. Union of India (2002): teaching about religions (not religious instruction) permissible.

Art 29(1): protection of language, script, culture of any section of citizens; 29(2): no denial of admission to any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving State aid on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language. Art 29 protects 'any section of citizens' - including majority (not only minorities).

Art 30(1): all minorities (religious or linguistic) have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Art 30(1A) (44th Amendment): compensation in case of compulsory acquisition of property of minority institutions must not restrict this right. Minority status determined State-wise (T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka, 2002, 11 judges); right of administration is not absolute - regulatory measures allowed to ensure excellence; no right to maladminister; unaided minority institutions can admit students of their choice with transparent merit-based process; P.A. Inamdar (2005) - no quota/reservation can be imposed on unaided private institutions.

S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India (1967) held AMU is not a minority institution; the 7-judge bench in Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (Nov 2024) overruled that reasoning (4:3) - an institution does not lose minority status merely because created by statute; the 'real' test is who established it, and the matter was sent back to a regular bench to apply the test [VERIFY later developments].
St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi (1992): minority institution can give preference to its community students, subject to reasonable limit; no complete exclusion of others.

key_provisions.content: Regulation of secular activities, social reform and opening of Hindu institutions to all Hindus.
Rights of denominations - 4 clauses (a)-(d).
Freedom from attending religious instruction.
Minorities' right to establish and administer educational institutions.

sections.title: Right to Property (Art 300A), Savings of Certain Laws (Arts 31A-31C), Constitutional Remedies and Writs (Arts 32-35, 226)
sections.overview: Writ jurisdiction is a constant AIBE theme (nature of each writ, scope of Art 32 vs 226). Property after 1978 is a constitutional right under Art 300A.
must_know: Art 32: right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of FR - itself a fundamental right; Dr Ambedkar called it 'the heart and soul of the Constitution'; part of basic structure. Supreme Court may issue directions, orders or writs including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari. Art 32(3): Parliament can empower other courts to issue writs. Art 32(4): right cannot be suspended except as provided by the Constitution.

Art 226: High Courts may issue writs to any person or authority (including Government) within its territorial jurisdiction - for enforcement of FR AND 'for any other purpose' - wider than Art 32. 226(1A): jurisdiction on the basis of cause of action arising wholly or partly in the territory (15th Amendment). Alternative remedy is a rule of prudence, not an absolute bar (Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, 1998 - exceptions: FR violation, natural justice breach, lack of jurisdiction, challenge to vires of law).

Habeas corpus ('produce the body'): against illegal detention by State or private persons; can be filed by any person; res judicata not applicable (Ghulam Sarwar, 1967). Mandamus ('we command'): to perform public duty; not against private individuals (generally), the President/Governors personally (Art 361), or for enforcing non-statutory directives; the petitioner must have legal right. Prohibition: issued to lower court/tribunal to prevent excess of jurisdiction - issued BEFORE the order is final (vs certiorari after order). Certiorari ('to be certified'): quash orders of inferior courts and quasi-judicial authorities for jurisdictional error, violation of natural justice, error of law apparent on face of record (Hari Vishnu Kamath, 1955; Syed Yakoob, 1964). Quo warranto ('by what authority'): against usurpation of public office of substantive character; any person can file (University of Mysore v. C.D. Govinda Rao, 1965).
Art 227: superintendence of High Courts over all courts and tribunals in its territory - basic structure (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997); Art 227 is wider (supervisory), non-writ.
Res judicata: dismissal of Art 226 petition on merits bars Art 32 petition on same facts (Daryao v. State of U.P., 1961); dismissal in limine without speaking order does not.

Locus standi relaxed for PIL: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981); Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984); Judges transfer case. 'Epistolary jurisdiction' - letters treated as petitions (Sunil Batra). Safeguards: Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010); misuse - 'publicity interest litigation' - costs imposed. [Cross-ref: Part 9 PIL.]

Art 33: Parliament may restrict/abrogate FR of armed forces, police, intelligence, etc. Art 34: restrictions on FR while martial law is in force; Parliament can indemnify. Art 35: only Parliament (not States) can make laws for giving effect to Arts 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 and offences under Part III.

Art 31 (compulsory acquisition) deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978); Art 19(1)(f) deleted; right to property now an ordinary constitutional right under Art 300A: 'No person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.' Judicial review is still available; compensation not guaranteed explicitly, but see Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar (1995) and Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah (2024) - Art 300A includes: duty to inform, hear objections, reasoned decision, public purpose, compensation, efficient acquisition, conclusion; it is also a human right.

sections.title: Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) and Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A)
sections.overview: Know classification, key Articles (39, 39A, 40, 41, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 48A, 50), relationship with FR, and the list of 11 fundamental duties.
must_know: Art 36: 'State' same as Part III. Art 37: DPSP are not enforceable by any court but are fundamental in the governance of the country; State has a duty to apply them in making laws.
Classification: Socialistic (Arts 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47); Gandhian (Arts 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48); Liberal-intellectual (Arts 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51).

Art 38: social order for promotion of welfare (38(2) minimise inequalities - 44th Amendment). Art 39: (a) adequate means of livelihood; (b) distribution of material resources to subserve common good; (c) prevent concentration of wealth; (d) equal pay for equal work for men and women; (e) health and strength of workers, no abuse of children; (f) opportunities for children to develop in healthy manner (42nd Amendment substituted).

Art 39A (42nd Amendment): equal justice and free legal aid. Art 40: village panchayats. Art 41: right to work, education and public assistance (within economic capacity). Art 42: just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Art 43: living wage; Art 43A (42nd): workers' participation in management; Art 43B (97th): cooperative societies.

Art 44: Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout India. Cases: Shah Bano (1985); Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995); John Vallamattom v. Union of India (2003); Shayara Bano (2017). Goa has a UCC (Portuguese Civil Code); Uttarakhand enacted a UCC in 2024 [VERIFY current status of rules/implementation].

Art 45 (86th Amendment, 2002): early childhood care and education for children below 6. Art 46: promote educational and economic interests of SC/ST and weaker sections. Art 47: raise level of nutrition and standard of living; improve public health; prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs. Art 48: organise agriculture and animal husbandry; prohibit slaughter of cows and other milch/draught cattle (State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat, 2005 upheld total ban). Art 48A (42nd): protect and improve environment, safeguard forests and wildlife. Art 49: protect monuments of national importance. Art 50: separate judiciary from executive. Art 51: promote international peace and security.

Relation with FR: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) - FR prevail over DPSP; Kesavananda (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) - harmony and balance between FR and DPSP is basic structure; neither has absolute primacy. DPSP can be used to interpret and expand FR (e.g., Art 21 through Art 39A, 41, 42, 47, 48A). Art 31C protects laws implementing Art 39(b)-(c).

Fundamental Duties (Art 51A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee). Originally 10; the 11th ((k) - parent/guardian to provide opportunities for education to child between 6 and 14) was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). Duties include: abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, national flag and anthem; cherish ideals of freedom struggle; uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity; defend the country; promote harmony and brotherhood; preserve rich heritage of composite culture; protect and improve natural environment (g); develop scientific temper, humanism; safeguard public property and abjure violence (i); strive for excellence (j); (k) education duty.

Duties are non-justiciable but are relevant in interpreting statutes and in testing reasonableness of restrictions (Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P., 1986; AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS, 2001; M.C. Mehta cases on environment).

sections.title: Union Executive: President, Vice-President, Council of Ministers, Attorney General
sections.overview: Election, qualification, impeachment, ordinance, pardon and aid-and-advice questions recur. Numbers (35 years, 14 days, 1/4, 2/3, 6 months, 15%) are the score-makers.
must_know: Art 52-53: President is head of the Union; executive power vested in President, exercised directly or through officers. Art 54: elected by an electoral college of ELECTED members of both Houses of Parliament and ELECTED members of Legislative Assemblies of States (including Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members and Legislative Council members do not vote. Art 55: system of proportional representation by single transferable vote, secret ballot. Disputes about the election: Supreme Court alone (Art 71).

Art 56: term 5 years; continues until successor enters office. Re-election allowed. Resignation to Vice-President. Art 57: eligible for re-election. Art 58 qualifications: citizen of India, completed 35 years, qualified for election as Lok Sabha member, holds no office of profit. Art 59: oath before the Chief Justice of India (Art 60).

Art 61 impeachment: only for 'violation of the Constitution'; charge by either House on a resolution moved after 14 days' written notice signed by at least one-fourth of total membership; passed by two-thirds of TOTAL membership; other House investigates; President has the right to appear/be represented; if the other House also passes by two-thirds of total membership, President is removed from the date of passing. Nominated members can participate.

Art 62: election to fill a vacancy within 6 months; Art 65: VP acts as President (up to the end of vacancy); Art 70: Parliament may make other provisions. Art 71: SC decides doubts/disputes; election cannot be challenged on the ground of vacancy in the electoral college.

Art 72 - pardoning power of President: pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, suspension, commutation - for offences by court martial; offences against Union law; death sentence. Judicially reviewable on limited grounds (Maru Ram, 1980; Kehar Singh v. Union of India, 1989 - President may scrutinise evidence afresh; Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt of A.P., 2006). Exercised on aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. Courts cannot examine merits; reasons need not be given. Compare Art 161 (Governor cannot pardon death sentence or court martial sentence).

Art 74: Council of Ministers with PM at head to aid and advise the President (42nd Amendment made advice binding; 44th Amendment allows President to ask for reconsideration once; second advice binding). Art 74(2): courts cannot inquire into the advice tendered. Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974): President and Governor are constitutional heads and act on ministerial advice except where Constitution expressly gives discretion.

Art 75: PM appointed by President; other ministers on PM's advice; ministers hold office during President's pleasure; collective responsibility to Lok Sabha (75(3)); total ministers not to exceed 15% of Lok Sabha strength (91st Amendment 2003; Art 75(1A)); a member disqualified under Tenth Schedule is also disqualified from being a minister (75(1B)); a non-member can be minister for 6 months (Art 75(5)). S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001): non-member cannot be re-appointed after 6 months without being elected.

Art 76: Attorney General - qualified to be SC judge; appointed by President; holds office during pleasure; right to speak in Parliament (Art 88) but no vote. Solicitor General is not a constitutional office (statutory/administrative). Art 148: CAG (see 1.17).

Art 63-71 Vice-President: elected by electoral college of all members (elected AND nominated) of both Houses of Parliament; proportional representation by single transferable vote; qualifications - citizen, 35 years, qualified for Rajya Sabha, no office of profit; term 5 years; ex officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Art 64) with casting vote only (Art 100); removal (Art 67(b)) by resolution of Rajya Sabha passed by an effective majority (majority of all then members) and agreed to by Lok Sabha by simple majority, after 14 days' notice. Dhankhar resigned in July 2025; C.P. Radhakrishnan was elected the 15th Vice-President in Sept 2025 [VERIFY].

Legislative powers of President: summon, prorogue (Art 85), dissolve Lok Sabha; address (Art 86-87); nominate 12 to Rajya Sabha (Art 80(3)) - literature, science, art, social service; nominate 2 Anglo-Indians (discontinued by 104th Amendment); assent to Bills (Art 111) - absolute veto, suspensive veto (return once for reconsideration - not for Money Bill; must assent if re-passed); pocket veto (inaction - Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill 1986; not expressly provided).

Art 123 Ordinance: when Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that immediate action is necessary; same force as Act; must be laid before both Houses and ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from reassembly (or earlier on disapproving resolution); can be withdrawn at any time; cannot alter the Constitution; limitations same as Parliament. D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): repeated re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution; Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017): 7-judge bench - re-promulgation is constitutional fraud; legislative satisfaction is judicially reviewable to limited extent; ordinance-making is not an unfettered power. R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970): satisfaction of President under Art 123 is justiciable.

Art 143: advisory jurisdiction - on question of law or fact of public importance; the Court may decline to answer (Ayodhya reference, Ismail Faruqui 1994); opinion is not binding on the President but is of high persuasive value and (per Special Courts Bill, 1978 and Natural Resources Allocation, 2012) is binding on courts. 16th Presidential Reference (Art 143) on Arts 200/201 decided Nov 2025 - see Latest Developments.

key_provisions.content: Electoral college for Presidential election: elected members only.
Impeachment: violation of Constitution; 1/4 notice; 2/3 of total membership in each House.
Pardoning power of the President.
Advice by ministers cannot be inquired into by any court.
Council of Ministers not to exceed 15% of Lok Sabha strength.
Ordinance-making power of the President.

Vice-President's removal needs no impeachment - only Rajya Sabha resolution + LS consent.

sections.title: Parliament: Composition, Procedure, Privileges, Money Bills and Anti-Defection (Tenth Schedule)
sections.overview: Composition numbers, joint sitting, Money Bill, privileges (Sita Soren) and anti-defection law (Kihoto Hollohan, Speaker timelines) are consistently tested.
must_know: Art 79: Parliament = President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha. Rajya Sabha (Art 80): maximum 250 (238 elected by State/UT legislatures + 12 nominated); present strength 245 (233 elected + 12 nominated); term 6 years; one-third retire every second year; permanent House; not subject to dissolution. Lok Sabha (Art 81): maximum 550 (530 from States + 20 from UTs); present strength 543; term 5 years (Art 83(2)); can be extended by Parliament for one year at a time during a proclamation of Emergency (not beyond 6 months after Emergency ends).

Qualifications (Art 84): citizen; age 25 (LS), 30 (RS); other qualifications by law (RP Act 1951). Disqualifications (Art 102): office of profit (Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India, 2006; 'Office of Profit' (Prevention of Disqualification) Act), unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, not a citizen, disqualified by law or Tenth Schedule. Decision on disqualification: President on the opinion of Election Commission (Art 103), except Tenth Schedule cases decided by the Speaker/Chairman.

RP Act 1951 s.8(3): conviction with imprisonment of 2 years or more = disqualification for term + 6 years. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013): s.8(4) (3-month protection) struck down - disqualification is immediate on conviction. Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2018). Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India (2019): Court refused to add disqualification at the charge-framing stage.

Art 85: sessions - not more than six months between two sessions. Art 87: special address by President. Art 93-96: Speaker and Deputy Speaker - elected by Lok Sabha, resign to each other; removal by resolution passed by an effective majority of all then members after 14 days' notice. Speaker has a casting vote only (Art 100(1)); presiding officer does not vote at first instance. Quorum = one-tenth of total membership (Art 100(3)). Deputy Speaker has been vacant in the 17th and 18th Lok Sabha - a debated violation of constitutional spirit [VERIFY current].

Legislative procedure: ordinary Bill - passes both Houses; Art 108 joint sitting for deadlock (if other House rejects, or disagrees on amendments, or six months lapse without passing) - presided by Speaker; applicable to ordinary and financial (non-money) Bills, NOT Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills. Joint sittings held: 1961 (Dowry Prohibition Bill), 1978 (Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill), 2002 (POTA).

Money Bill (Art 110): introduced only in Lok Sabha on President's recommendation; Speaker's certificate is final (Art 110(3)); Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments within 14 days (Art 109); LS may accept or reject. Financial Bill (Art 117) - Category I (money-bill-like provisions + others) and Category II. Aadhaar Act, 2016 passed as Money Bill: validity upheld in Puttaswamy (2018) majority, doubted by minority; Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank (2019) referred the issue of Money Bill certification to a larger bench - pending [VERIFY].

Budget process: Art 112 (annual financial statement), 113 (voting on demands for grants - only Lok Sabha), 114 (Appropriation Bill), 115 (supplementary), 116 (vote on account), 117; 265 - no tax except by authority of law; 266 - Consolidated Fund of India/State and Public Account; 267 - Contingency Fund of India (corpus Rs 500 crore, earlier Rs 50 crore) at disposal of the President.

Privileges: Art 105(1) freedom of speech in Parliament; 105(2) no liability in any court for anything said or any vote given in Parliament or its committees, and for publication under authority of a House; 105(3) other privileges defined by law (not yet codified) as of 44th Amendment commencement. Art 122 - validity of proceedings cannot be questioned on irregularity of procedure. Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007): expulsion of MPs in 'cash for query' sting upheld; privilege action is subject to limited judicial review. Keshav Singh (1965) - Art 143 reference on conflict between Assembly and HC; Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959) - privileges not subject to Art 19(1)(a).

P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (CBI/SPE) (1998) (3:2) gave MPs immunity from prosecution for taking bribes for votes; OVERRULED by the 7-judge Bench in Sita Soren v. Union of India (4 March 2024): bribery is not protected by Art 105(2)/194(2); no immunity from prosecution for receiving bribe to vote or speak in a certain way.

Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment 1985; modified by 91st Amendment 2003 to omit split exception): disqualification if a member voluntarily gives up membership of party or votes/abstains contrary to party whip without permission (unless condoned within 15 days); independent members joining a party; nominated members joining a party after 6 months. Exception: merger of two-thirds of legislature party with another party (para 4). Decision by the Speaker/Chairman (para 6).

Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): Tenth Schedule valid; para 7 (ousting court jurisdiction) struck down for lacking ratification under Art 368(2)(ii); Speaker's decision is a tribunal decision subject to judicial review on limited grounds (jurisdictional errors, mala fides, perversity, violation of natural justice) and cannot be reviewed before the final decision except for interim disqualification/suspension. Ravi S. Naik (1994): 'voluntarily giving up membership' includes conduct inferred; Rajendra Singh Rana (2007); Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur Legislative Assembly (2020): Speaker must decide within 3 months ordinarily; Parliament should consider vesting the power in an independent tribunal. Padi Kaushik Reddy v. State of Telangana (July 2025): Speaker directed to decide within 3 months [VERIFY]. Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Maharashtra (2023, 5 judges): Governor cannot call a floor test without objective material; whip of a political party (not legislature party) is the relevant authority; Nabam Rebia (2016) reference to 7 judges left to be examined.

Women's reservation: Constitution (106th Amendment) Act 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) - one-third reservation of seats for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Delhi Assembly (Arts 330A, 332A, 239AA(2)(b)); to come into force after the first census and delimitation exercise after commencement; 15-year duration, extendable. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill 2026 on delimitation and operationalisation was defeated in the Lok Sabha (April 2026) for want of two-thirds majority [VERIFY details].

sections.title: State Executive and Legislature: Governor, Chief Minister, Legislative Council
sections.overview: Governor's powers (esp. Arts 161, 163, 174, 200, 213) and the recent controversy over assent to Bills dominate.
must_know: Art 153-155: Governor appointed by the President by warrant; Art 156: holds office during the pleasure of the President, normal term 5 years (B.P. Singhal v. Union of India, 2010 - no removal without compelling reasons; no reasons need be disclosed but arbitrary removal reviewable). Art 157: citizen of India, age 35. Art 158: no office of profit, no membership of Legislature.

Art 163: Council of Ministers headed by CM aids and advises Governor except where Governor is required to act in his discretion (e.g., Art 239(2), Sixth Schedule, 371-series). Art 164: CM appointed by Governor; other ministers on CM's advice; ministers hold office during Governor's pleasure; collective responsibility to Assembly; ministers not exceeding 15% of Assembly strength (minimum 12 in a State) - 91st Amendment; Art 164(4) non-member minister for 6 months.

Art 161: Governor's power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions or suspend, remit or commute sentences for offences against State laws; cannot pardon a death sentence (only suspend, remit or commute it) or court-martial sentence. Art 167: CM's duty to inform the Governor; Art 165: Advocate-General.

Art 174: Governor summons, prorogues and dissolves Assembly - acts on advice of Council of Ministers (Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, 2016 - Governor cannot summon the Assembly at his own discretion; Subhash Desai, 2023).

Art 200 - assent to Bills: Governor may (i) assent; (ii) withhold assent (money bills: cannot return); (iii) return a non-money Bill with a message for reconsideration; (iv) reserve for President's consideration (compulsory for Bills affecting High Court's position under proviso). If re-passed, Governor shall not withhold assent. Art 201: President may assent, withhold, or return the Bill (if not Money Bill) for reconsideration; no timelines in the text. See Latest Developments for Nov 2025 opinion.

Art 213: Governor's ordinance-making power when Legislature is not in session; ceases six weeks after reassembly; requires prior instructions of President in certain cases (e.g., Bill that would need President's previous sanction).

State Legislature: Art 168; Art 169 - creation or abolition of Legislative Council by Parliament by law after Assembly resolution passed by majority of total membership and two-thirds of present and voting (not an Art 368 amendment). Councils currently exist in 6 States: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh. Strength of Council cannot exceed one-third of Assembly and not less than 40 (Art 171). Assembly: 60 to 500 members (Art 170); exceptions e.g., Goa, Sikkim, Mizoram (min 30). Term: 5 years (Art 172); Council is permanent with one-third retiring every 2 years; Council has no power over Money Bills (can delay 14 days, Art 198); Governor nominates one-sixth of Council members.
Art 212 - courts shall not enquire into proceedings of Legislature; Art 194 - privileges; Art 208 - rules of procedure; Art 207 - financial bills.

Art 356 President's Rule: where Governor reports (or otherwise) that the government cannot be carried on per Constitution; Union takes over State functions; Parliament's approval within 2 months by simple majority of both Houses; initial 6 months; extended in 6-month increments up to a maximum of 3 years; beyond 1 year only if (a) national emergency is in operation and (b) Election Commission certifies difficulties in elections (Art 356(5), 44th Amendment). S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994, 9 judges): proclamation is justiciable; floor test is the only way to test majority; Assembly cannot be dissolved before Parliamentary approval ('suspended animation'); misuse by Centre can be set aside and status quo ante restored; Art 356 cannot be used for secularism-related failings absent constitutional breakdown except where a State acts against secularism, a basic feature.

Delhi and Puducherry: Art 239AA (69th Amendment 1991) - NCT of Delhi has Legislative Assembly; Union and Delhi: State of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018, 5 judges - LG bound by aid & advice save for land, police, public order) and Govt of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (May 2023, 5 judges - Delhi government has executive and legislative control over 'services' except police, public order, land); Parliament passed the GNCTD (Amendment) Act 2023 overriding the verdict - challenge pending [VERIFY].

key_provisions.content: Governor's pardoning power - not death sentence pardon, not court-martial.
Aid and advice of Council of Ministers; discretionary functions.
Governor's options on Bills passed by State Legislature.
Ordinances by Governor.

sections.title: The Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts, Subordinate Courts, Tribunals, Collegium, Contempt
sections.overview: Jurisdictions of SC (original, appellate, advisory, special leave, review), judges' appointment and removal, Collegium cases, Art 142 and tribunals.
must_know: Art 124: Supreme Court of India; judges appointed by President after consultation with such SC and HC judges as the President deems necessary; CJI always consulted for others (Art 124(2)). Sanctioned strength 34 including CJI (2019 amendment to the 1956 Act); reports in 2026 indicate an increase to 38 via ordinance [VERIFY]. Qualification (Art 124(3)): citizen; at least 5 years as HC judge, or 10 years as HC advocate, or distinguished jurist (in President's opinion). Retirement at 65; HC at 62. Salaries are charged on Consolidated Fund and cannot be varied to disadvantage (Art 125).

Removal (Art 124(4)-(5)): by President on an address by each House supported by a majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968. No judge has been successfully removed (Justice V. Ramaswami, 1993, motion failed). Art 121: no discussion in Parliament on conduct of a judge except on removal motion.

Appointments - Judges cases: First Judges case (S.P. Gupta, 1981): 'consultation' does not mean concurrence; executive primacy. Second Judges case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India, 1993, 9 judges): CJI's opinion has primacy; 'consultation' = 'concurrence'; collegium of CJI + 2 senior-most judges. Third Judges case (Special Reference No. 1 of 1998, Art 143): collegium expanded to CJI + 4 senior-most judges (SC) and CJI + 2 senior-most judges for HC; Fourth Judges case (SCAORA, 2015): 99th Amendment (Art 124A, NJAC) held unconstitutional (4:1) - independence of judiciary is basic structure; Justice Chelameswar dissented.

SC jurisdiction: Art 32 (writs), Art 131 (original - disputes between Centre and State(s) or between States on a question of law or fact involving legal right; excludes private parties; Art 131 does not cover pre-Constitution treaties); Art 132-134 (appeals in constitutional, civil, criminal matters; Art 134A certificate); Art 136 (Special Leave Petition - discretionary, not confined to HC judgments, can be against any court/tribunal except military tribunals - Art 136(2)); Art 137 (review), Art 139 (writs for purposes other than FR); Art 139A (transfer of cases); Art 141 (law declared by SC is binding on all courts in India); Art 142 (complete justice - Union Carbide Corp v. Union of India 1991; Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India 1998 - cannot override express statutory prohibition or substantive law; used for dissolution of marriage on irretrievable breakdown in Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan, 2023); Art 143 (advisory); Art 144 (civil and judicial authorities to aid SC); Art 129 (SC is a court of record with power to punish for contempt); Art 145 (rules); Art 147 (interpretation - substantial question of law as to Constitution - at least 5 judges, Art 145(3)).

High Courts: Art 214 - HC for each State; Art 215 - court of record; Art 216 - CJ and other judges; Art 217 - appointment by President after consultation with CJI, Governor and Chief Justice of HC; qualification (Art 217(2)): citizen, 10 years judicial office or 10 years HC advocate; retirement at 62; Art 222 transfer by President after consulting CJI; Art 224 additional/acting judges; Art 224A retired judges (ad hoc); Art 226 writs (see 1.9); Art 227 superintendence; Art 228 transfer of cases involving substantial questions of law; Art 231 common HC for two or more States. Presently 25 High Courts.

Subordinate courts: Art 233 - District Judge appointed by the Governor in consultation with the HC; qualification - not in service, advocate for 7 years and recommended by HC (Chandra Mohan v. State of U.P., 1966). Art 234 - recruitment of persons other than DJ; Art 235 - control over subordinate judiciary vests in the HC (disciplinary control); Art 236-237; Art 247 - Parliament may create additional courts; Art 312 - All India Judicial Service.

Tribunals: Art 323A (administrative tribunals), 323B (other tribunals) inserted by the 42nd Amendment; Administrative Tribunals Act 1985; L. Chandra Kumar (1997): exclusion of HC jurisdiction struck down; tribunals are subject to judicial review by HC (Division Bench). Madras Bar Association cases: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 provisions were struck down in 2021 and again in 2025 [VERIFY].

Contempt: Contempt of Courts Act 1971 - civil and criminal contempt; punishment: simple imprisonment up to 6 months, fine up to Rs 2,000 or both; s.13 (truth as defence if bona fide and public interest - 2006 amendment); limitation 1 year (s.20). SC and HC are courts of record (Arts 129, 215). Re: Prashant Bhushan (2020): fine of Re 1. In re Arundhati Roy (2002).

Judicial review types and basic features: judicial review is basic structure (Kesavananda, L. Chandra Kumar, Minerva Mills). Separation of powers is basic structure. Court cannot legislate but may fill vacuum through guidelines (Vishaka), and Art 142 powers. Doctrine of Judicial restraint and non-justiciability of political questions (e.g., Art 74(2)).

CJI: Justice Surya Kant became the 53rd Chief Justice of India on 24 Nov 2025; retirement due 9 Feb 2027 [VERIFY]. Appointment of CJI by seniority (Memorandum of Procedure); President is bound to appoint the senior-most.
