sections.title: Centre-State Relations: Legislative, Administrative, Financial; Trade and Commerce; Inter-State Disputes
sections.overview: Seventh Schedule lists, doctrines (pith and substance, repugnancy), Art 249/250/252/253, Art 254, GST Council and Finance Commission are standard MCQ topics.
must_know: Art 245: Parliament for whole/part of India; State legislature for its State; Parliament's laws can have extra-territorial operation (Art 245(2)). Art 246: Union List (List I - about 100 entries), State List (List II - about 61 entries), Concurrent List (List III - about 52 entries); Parliament's exclusive power over List I; State exclusive over List II; both over List III; Parliament has overriding power. Art 248 and List I Entry 97: residuary power vests in Parliament (Canadian model).

42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects from State List to Concurrent List: education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, administration of justice. Art 246A (101st Amendment): both Parliament and State legislatures can make laws on GST; Parliament has exclusive power on inter-State supply of goods/services.

Doctrine of pith and substance (State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, 1951; Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee, 1947): incidental encroachment is permissible if the true nature of the law falls within the legislature's list. Doctrine of colourable legislation (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, 1953): what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. Doctrine of harmonious construction, occupied field and territorial nexus (State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala, 1957).

Art 254 - repugnancy between Union and State law on Concurrent List: Union law prevails and State law is void to the extent of repugnancy; exception under Art 254(2) - if State law was reserved for the President and received assent, State law prevails in that State, but Parliament can subsequently override it by law. Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay (1954); M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979) - tests of repugnancy: direct inconsistency, occupied field.

Exceptional Parliamentary powers over State List: Art 249 (national interest - Rajya Sabha resolution passed by two-thirds of members present and voting; law operates for up to 1 year, extendable year by year); Art 250 (during Emergency); Art 252 (consent of two or more States by resolution; others may adopt - e.g., Prize Competitions Act); Art 253 (to implement treaties, international agreements or decisions - Union can legislate on any subject); Art 258-A; Art 356(1)(b).

Administrative relations: Art 256 - States to comply with Union laws; Art 257 - Union can give directions; Art 258 - delegation of Union functions to States; Art 261 - full faith and credit to public acts, records, and judicial proceedings; Art 262 - adjudication of inter-State water disputes (Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956); Art 263 - Inter-State Council (established 1990 on Sarkaria Commission's recommendation). All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFS) - Art 312. Zonal Councils are statutory (States Reorganisation Act 1956), not constitutional. Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) and Punchhi Commission (2007-10) reports on Centre-State relations.

Financial relations: Art 264-267, 268 (duties levied by Union, collected and appropriated by States - stamp duties), 269-270 (Union-levied taxes shared with States - income tax other than agricultural income, GST/IGST), 271 (surcharge - Union only), 272 (omitted), 273-275 (grants-in-aid - Art 275 statutory grants; Art 282 discretionary grants), 280 (Finance Commission - constituted every 5 years by President; chairman + 4 members; recommends distribution of net proceeds of taxes), 281, 292-293 (borrowings), 285-289 (immunities: Union property exempt from State tax (Art 285), State property from Union tax (Art 289)).

Finance Commissions: 15th FC (chair N.K. Singh) - States' share in divisible pool 41% for 2021-26. 16th FC (chair Arvind Panagariya; constituted Dec 2023) - award period 2026-31; recommendations tabled with the Union Budget 2026-27 [VERIFY particulars before exam].

GST: Art 279A (101st Amendment 2016) - GST Council chaired by Union Finance Minister with State finance ministers; decisions by 3/4 weighted majority (Centre one-third weight; States two-thirds); Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2022): GST Council recommendations are not binding but persuasive; Parliament and States have simultaneous power under Art 246A.

Trade and commerce (Part XIII): Art 301 - free trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India; Art 302 - Parliament may impose restrictions in public interest; Art 303 - no discrimination between States; Art 304 - State may impose non-discriminatory taxes / reasonable restrictions (with President's previous sanction for the Bill under 304(b)); Art 305; Art 307 - authority to carry out purposes of Arts 301-304. Cases: Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam (1961); Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) v. State of Rajasthan (1962) - regulatory and compensatory measures do not violate Art 301.

Art 298-300: executive power to carry on trade; Art 299 - contracts by Union/State must be expressed to be made by the President/Governor and executed by authorised persons (Bhikraj Jaipuria v. Union of India, 1962; Mulamchand v. State of M.P., 1968 - s.70 Contract Act remedy). Art 300: suits and proceedings by or against the Government; Art 300A - property. Art 361: President/Governor immunity; civil proceedings need 2 months' notice (Art 361(4)).

sections.title: Emergency Provisions (Part XVIII: Arts 352-360)
sections.overview: Three types of emergencies; conditions of declaration and approval; effect on FR; 44th Amendment safeguards; Bommai on Art 356.
must_know: National Emergency (Art 352): on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion ('internal disturbance' replaced by 'armed rebellion' - 44th Amendment 1978). President can proclaim on the written recommendation of the Cabinet (Art 352(3)). Must be approved by both Houses within one month by a special majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting); lasts 6 months, renewable indefinitely with approval every six months by simple majority. Revoked by President or by Lok Sabha resolution; one-tenth of LS members may requisition a special sitting to disapprove (Art 352(8)). Judicial review: limited, on grounds of mala fides/extraneous reasons (Minerva Mills 1980).

Effects: Centre can give directions to States on any matter (Art 353); Parliament can legislate on State List (Art 250); LS term extendable by a year at a time (Art 83(2)); Art 354 - revenue distribution may be modified; Art 358 - Art 19 is automatically suspended only on Emergency grounds of war/external aggression (not armed rebellion); Art 359 - President may suspend the right to move court for enforcement of specified FR; Arts 20 and 21 cannot be suspended (44th Amendment). Emergency has been declared in 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pakistan war) and 1975 (internal disturbance - 25 June 1975 to 21 March 1977). The Union notified 25 June as 'Samvidhan Hatya Diwas' in 2024.
ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976): during Emergency, right to habeas corpus is suspended - widely condemned; overruled in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017). Justice H.R. Khanna's dissent is celebrated.

State Emergency/President's Rule (Art 356): see Section 1.13 and Bommai. Art 355: duty of Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance and ensure State government is according to the Constitution. Art 365: failure to comply with Union directions can trigger Art 356.

Financial Emergency (Art 360): when financial stability or credit of India or any part is threatened; approval by Parliament within 2 months by simple majority; lasts until revoked; President can direct States to observe financial principles, reduce salaries of all persons in government service (including judges of SC and HC). Never declared yet.

Art 356 usage: Duration - 6 months, extendable to 3 years max; in practice over 130 invocations; S.R. Bommai (1994) curbed misuse. Art 356 imposed on Manipur from 13 Feb 2025 and extended [VERIFY current status].

sections.title: Services, Commissions and Constitutional Bodies; Elections; Special Provisions; Languages; Miscellaneous
sections.overview: Art 311 protection of civil servants, Election Commission and the 2023 Act, CAG, UPSC, language provisions and special-status Articles are common.
must_know: Art 309-311 (Part XIV): Art 309 - recruitment and conditions by law; Art 310 - doctrine of pleasure (civil servants hold office at the pleasure of the President/Governor, subject to Art 311); Art 311(1) - no dismissal or removal by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority; Art 311(2) - no dismissal, removal or reduction in rank except after an inquiry with reasonable opportunity to be heard; exceptions (second proviso): conviction on criminal charge; where inquiry is impracticable; security of the State. Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985); Shamsher Singh (1974).

Art 312 All-India Services - Parliament may create by RS resolution (2/3 of present and voting): Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), Indian Forest Service. Art 315-323 Public Service Commissions: UPSC - chairman and members appointed by President, term 6 years or 65 years; State PSC - appointed by Governor, 6 years or 62 years; removal only by the President after SC inquiry on grounds of misbehaviour (Art 317) or by order for insolvency, outside employment, or unfitness. Art 320 consultation functions; Art 323 reports.

Art 324: Election Commission - superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State legislatures, offices of President and Vice-President. Article 324(5): CEC removal only in same manner and on same grounds as SC judge; other ECs removed only on CEC's recommendation. Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (March 2023, 5 judges): until Parliament legislates, CEC/EC appointment by committee of PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act 2023 replaced the CJI with a Union Cabinet minister nominated by PM - challenge pending [VERIFY]. Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1978): Art 324 has residuary powers subject to law; Art 329(b): no court interference in electoral matters once notified (election petition is the only remedy). Art 326: universal adult suffrage (18 years - 61st Amendment, 1988). Art 327-328 laws on elections; Art 243K/243ZA local body elections by SEC.

Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls: Bihar SIR (June 2025) challenged before the SC (Association for Democratic Reforms v. ECI); the Court allowed Aadhaar as a 12th document by an interim order in Sept 2025; the final decision in 2026 upheld ECI's power to purify electoral rolls but stressed constitutional rights (right to vote under Art 326 is statutory-constitutional) [VERIFY final holding]. SIR was extended to other States from late 2025.

Art 148-151: CAG - appointed by President; removal like SC judge; term 6 years or 65; salary charged to Consolidated Fund; audits Union and State accounts (Art 149); reports to President/Governor placed before Parliament/Legislature (Art 151); 'friend, philosopher and guide' of PAC. Art 165 - Advocate General of State.

Art 330-342 Special provisions for SC/ST/Anglo-Indians: Art 330/332 - reservation of seats in LS/Assemblies for SC/ST; 104th Amendment (2019) extended SC/ST reservation to 2030 and discontinued Anglo-Indian nomination; Art 338 NCSC (65th Amendment); 338A NCST (89th Amendment); 338B NCBC (102nd Amendment, 2018); Art 339 - control of Union over administration of Scheduled Areas; Art 340 - Commission for backward classes (Kaka Kalelkar 1953; Mandal 1979); Art 341 - SC list by President (Parliament can modify); Art 342 - ST; Art 342A - President's list of SEBCs (102nd); Art 366(26C) SEBC definition; 105th Amendment restored State list power (2021). Art 335 - SC/ST claims to service consistent with efficiency.

Languages: Art 343 - Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union; English continued for 15 years (Art 343(2)-(3), Official Languages Act 1963 - English continues indefinitely until legislature decides otherwise; Art 344 Commission); Art 345 - State official language; Art 346-347; Art 348 - language of SC/HC proceedings and authoritative texts of laws - English; Art 349-350; Art 350A - mother tongue instruction at primary level; Art 350B - Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities; Art 351 - directive to develop Hindi. Eighth Schedule - 22 languages (Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali - 71st Amendment; Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali - 92nd Amendment; Sindhi - 21st; Odia spelling 96th). Classical language status (Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali added in Oct 2024) is administrative, not constitutional.

Special provisions for States: Art 370 (J&K) - abrogation of special status on 5 Aug 2019 upheld in In re: Article 370 of the Constitution (11 Dec 2023, 5 judges, unanimous): Art 370 was a temporary provision; President had power to issue Constitutional Order 273 declaring Art 370 inoperative; J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 valid insofar as it created UT of Ladakh; statehood to be restored as soon as possible; elections to the Assembly were to be held by 30 Sept 2024. Art 371 (Maharashtra, Gujarat), 371A (Nagaland - 13th Amendment), 371B (Assam), 371C (Manipur), 371D and 371E (Andhra Pradesh/Telangana), 371F (Sikkim - 36th Amendment), 371G (Mizoram - 53rd), 371H (Arunachal - 55th), 371I (Goa - 56th), 371J (Karnataka - Hyderabad-Karnataka - 98th Amendment).

Art 244, Fifth Schedule (administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram - Governor's powers), Sixth Schedule (tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram - autonomous district and regional councils); Art 244A (autonomous State in Assam). Samatha v. State of A.P. (1997): tribal land transfers; Orissa Mining Corp. v. MoEF (Niyamgiri, 2013): Gram Sabha consent.

Art 361: immunity of President and Governors - not answerable to any court for exercise and performance of official powers and duties; no criminal proceedings during term; civil proceedings after 2 months' notice. Art 300: suits against Government; Art 361A: protection of publication of legislative proceedings; Art 363-363A: privy purses abolished (26th Amendment 1971). Art 366 definitions; Art 367 interpretation; Art 368 amendment; Arts 369-392 temporary and transitional provisions.
Citizenship and other cross-links: Art 51A, Art 243. Art 50 separation of judiciary from executive.

sections.title: Local Self-Government, Co-operatives, Union Territories and Schedules
sections.overview: Short but scoring: 73rd/74th Amendments, Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules, 97th Amendment and the list of Schedules.
must_know: 73rd Amendment (1992, effective 24 April 1993 - National Panchayati Raj Day): Part IX (Arts 243-243O) and Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects). Three-tier system (village, intermediate, district; intermediate tier optional for States with population below 20 lakh); Gram Sabha (Art 243A); direct elections; fixed 5-year term; elections within 6 months of dissolution (Art 243E); one-third reservation for women (243D), SC/ST in proportion to population, reservation for chairpersons; State Election Commission (243K) conducts elections; State Finance Commission every 5 years (243I). PESA 1996 extends to Scheduled Areas. Exempt: Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, hill areas of Manipur, Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council.

74th Amendment (1992): Part IXA (Arts 243P-243ZG), Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects); municipalities: Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation; Wards Committees for population 3 lakh or more; metropolitan planning committee (243ZE) and district planning committee (243ZD).
97th Amendment (2011): Part IXB (Arts 243ZH-243ZT); cooperative societies made a fundamental right under Art 19(1)(c) and DPSP Art 43B; Rajendra Shah (2021).

sections.title: Constitutional Interpretation, Doctrines and Principles Frequently Tested
sections.overview: Doctrines that appear in MCQs as 'which doctrine is described?' or 'which case propounded?'.
must_know: Pith and substance - true nature of legislation (Balsara 1951). Colourable legislation - indirect exercise of power one does not have. Doctrine of harmonious construction. Doctrine of eclipse - pre-Constitution law dormant. Doctrine of severability. Doctrine of waiver - FR cannot be waived. Doctrine of territorial nexus - extra-territorial operation needs nexus with India (State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C.). Doctrine of repugnancy (Art 254). Doctrine of occupied field. Doctrine of basic structure (Kesavananda). Doctrine of prospective overruling (Golak Nath). Doctrine of legitimate expectation (Navjyoti Co-op Group Housing Society v. Union of India, 1992). Doctrine of proportionality (Modern Dental 2016; Puttaswamy 2017). Doctrine of pleasure (Art 310, Art 156, Art 76). Doctrine of 'ejusdem generis' and 'noscitur a sociis' used in interpretation. Doctrine of separation of powers - Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955), Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, Kesavananda. Doctrine of public trust (M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, 1997). Doctrine of 'law of the land' vs 'due process'.

Presumption of constitutionality of statutes; burden on the challenger (Ram Krishna Dalmia v. S.R. Tendolkar, 1958). Courts do not strike down a statute merely because it is harsh; no judicial review of wisdom of legislation. Laws are tested on: legislative competence (Arts 245-254), violation of FR (Part III), violation of other provisions, basic structure for amendments.

Rule of law (A.V. Dicey) - supremacy of law, equality before law, predominance of legal spirit; basic structure feature in Indian context. Separation of powers is not rigid in India but its essence is basic structure (In re Delhi Laws Act, 1951; Ram Jawaya Kapur). Delegation of legislative power - excessive delegation impermissible; essential legislative functions cannot be delegated (In re Delhi Laws Act 1951; Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India, 1960; Gwalior Rayon). Delegated legislation becomes enforceable only upon publication in the manner required by statute - Viraj Impex v. Union of India (2026) [VERIFY citation]. [Cross-ref: Part 8 Administrative Law.]

Federalism: Indian Constitution is 'federal in structure but unitary in spirit' - quasi-federal (K.C. Wheare). S.R. Bommai (1994): federalism is basic feature. State of W.B. v. Union of India (1962): States are not sovereign. 'Indestructible Union of destructible States' (Ambedkar). 'Cooperative federalism' and 'dialogic federalism' - evolved in recent Governor-assent opinions.

Secularism - 'positive secularism': the State maintains equal distance from all religions (S.R. Bommai, 1994). Democracy - free and fair elections is a basic feature. Judicial review is the heart of the Constitution.

latest_developments.topic: Presidential Reference on Governor/President assent to Bills (Arts 200, 201, 143)
latest_developments.date: Opinion delivered 20 Nov 2025 (five-judge Constitution Bench headed by CJI B.R. Gavai); Special Reference No. 1 of 2025
latest_developments.summary: In response to the President's 14 questions (13 May 2025), the Court held that no judicially fixed timelines can be imposed on Governors/Presidents for acting on Bills, and 'deemed assent' through Art 142 is not permissible because the Court cannot substitute a constitutional functionary. Decisions under Arts 200/201 are not justiciable on merits before a Bill becomes law; limited judicial intervention is possible for prolonged and unexplained inaction. The President need not seek an Art 143 reference on every reserved Bill. The opinion effectively disapproved the 8 April 2025 judgment in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu.
